A1-A2.headline: Our Beautiful Moon In The Night Sky

pages.text: The Moon is the only natural body that goes around Earth. It travels about 378,000 kilometers away every 29.5 days. Earth's pull holds its turn steady, so we always see the same side.
pages.caption: Moon

evidence.articleCaption: Moon

pages.text: Dark flat plains and round holes cover the Moon's face. Hot melted rock formed those dark plains long ago. Space rocks hit the surface and left fine grey dust behind. With no real air, old marks stay clear.
pages.caption: The heavily cratered surface of the Moon, particularly where no mare formed, is discernable when viewed close up, with crater ridges highlighted at the terminator and the two most prominent craters on the near side, Tycho (left) and Copernicus (top) visible, featuring long bright impact-streaks.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Gibbous Moon Highlighting the Tycho and Copernicus Craters.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: The heavily cratered surface of the Moon, particularly where no mare formed, is discernable when viewed close up, with crater ridges highlighted at the terminator and the two most prominent craters on the near side, Tycho (left) and Copernicus (top) visible, featuring long bright impact-streaks.

pages.text: The Moon shines as the brightest object in our night sky. Even so, its surface is dark like road stone. When Earth moves between the Sun and Moon, Earth's shadow covers the Moon in a dark sky show.
pages.caption: The monthly changes in the angle between the direction of sunlight and view from Earth, and the phases of the Moon that result, as viewed from the Northern Hemisphere. The Earth–Moon distance is not to scale.

evidence.articleCaption: The monthly changes in the angle between the direction of sunlight and view from Earth, and the phases of the Moon that result, as viewed from the Northern Hemisphere. The Earth–Moon distance is not to scale.

pages.text: Long ago, people told old stories about the Moon. Later, robotic probes flew there first. In 1969, Apollo 11 landed the first humans on the Moon. Scientists study its 4.35-billion-year past and look for water.
pages.caption: Distribution of surface ice at the Moon's South (left) and North poles (right), as viewed by NASA's Moon Mineralogy Mapper (M) spectrometer onboard India's Chandrayaan-1 orbiter

evidence.fileTitle: File:The image shows the distribution of surface ice at the Moon's south pole (left) and north pole (right).webp
evidence.articleCaption: Distribution of surface ice at the Moon's South (left) and North poles (right), as viewed by NASA's Moon Mineralogy Mapper (M) spectrometer onboard India's Chandrayaan-1 orbiter

pages.text: Ocean pulls slowly push the Moon a little farther from Earth each year. Billions of years from now, the Sun will grow huge and red. That big change will disturb the quiet dance of Earth and the Moon.
pages.caption: Artist's depiction of the Moon in Earth's sky as it might have appeared around 4 billion years ago, after the Late Heavy Bombardment. At that time the Moon orbited the Earth at a third of its current distance, making it appear 2.8 times larger in apparent size than it does today.

C1-C2.headline: The Lunar Legacy: Unraveling The Moon's Geologic And Cosmic History

pages.text: As Earth's sole natural satellite, the Moon traverses an elliptical orbit averaging 378,000 kilometers every 29.5 days. Gravitational tidal locking synchronizes its rotation, permanently orienting one hemisphere toward Earth.
pages.caption: Moon

evidence.articleCaption: Moon

pages.text: Differentiated into crust, mantle, and core from a primordial magma ocean, the lunar surface preserves ancient basaltic maria, impact basins, and pulverized regolith virtually unaltered in the absence of a substantial atmosphere.
pages.caption: The heavily cratered surface of the Moon, particularly where no mare formed, is discernable when viewed close up, with crater ridges highlighted at the terminator and the two most prominent craters on the near side, Tycho (left) and Copernicus (top) visible, featuring long bright impact-streaks.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Gibbous Moon Highlighting the Tycho and Copernicus Craters.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: The heavily cratered surface of the Moon, particularly where no mare formed, is discernable when viewed close up, with crater ridges highlighted at the terminator and the two most prominent craters on the near side, Tycho (left) and Copernicus (top) visible, featuring long bright impact-streaks.

pages.text: Despite a remarkably low albedo resembling weathered asphalt, the Moon dominates nocturnal luminance. Earth's umbra generates lunar eclipses, whereas its apparent angular parity with the Sun enables rare total solar eclipses.
pages.caption: The monthly changes in the angle between the direction of sunlight and view from Earth, and the phases of the Moon that result, as viewed from the Northern Hemisphere. The Earth–Moon distance is not to scale.

pages.text: Moving from mythological veneration to astronautical exploration, robotic Luna probes preceded Apollo 11's 1969 crewed landing. Ongoing missions analyze its 4.35-billion-year history while prospecting polar ice for future bases.
pages.caption: Distribution of surface ice at the Moon's South (left) and North poles (right), as viewed by NASA's Moon Mineralogy Mapper (M) spectrometer onboard India's Chandrayaan-1 orbiter

pages.text: Secular tidal dissipation steadily widens the Earth-Moon orbital separation. Billions of years hence, solar expansion into a red giant will destabilize this partnership, potentially disintegrating the Moon near its Roche limit.
